parsing_res_list.block_content: The amount of composite action between the reinforcing steel and masonry is very dependent on the workmanship during wall construction including the grout placement,since the grout transfers the tension strength of the reinforcing steel into the wall. This has been demonstrated in blast test programs on reinforced masonry walls, where walls with careful inspection during construction demonstrated significantly greater blast resistance than walls with no inspection (Oswald, et al 2006). Full composite action is necessary for reinforced masonry to develop a ductile resisting moment based on the dynamic tensile yield strength of reinforcement and the compression strength of the masonry, as assumed for blast design.

All blast resistant reinforced masonry walls should be subject to inspection and material testing during construction as required in Chapter 1 of TMS 402/ACI 530/ASCE 5 for essential facilities (i.e. Level C Quality Assurance). This requirement helps ensure that the reinforcing steel and surrounding grout will be constructed to act compositely with the surrounding masonry before and after yielding of the steel and that there are no voids in solid grouted walls that are intended to provide protection from fragments.Procedures that inhibit full composite action include insufficient vibrating during placement, improper reinforcing steel placement too near an edge of the grouted space,mortar protrusion and droppings into the grouted space, and grout with insufficient strength or plasticity. Additionally, both vertical and horizontal reinforcement should be accurately positioned during wall construction and rigidly secured at intervals by wire ties or spacing devices. The distance between reinforcement and the masonry unit must not be less than -inch for fine grout or /-inch for course grout.

The ultimate dynamic moment capacity used to calculate the resistance of reinforced masonry walls is shown in Equation 6-9. This equation assumes that reinforced masonry will respond in essentially the same manner to blast loading as reinforced concrete. The applicability of this assumption has been demonstrated in numerous static tests and blast tests on well constructed reinforced masonry walls.

$M_{u}=$ dynamic ultimate moment capacity per unit width 
$A_{s}=$ area of tension reinforcement in width, b 
$\pmb{f}_{d y}=$ dynamic design stress 

$d=$ effective depth (distance from the extreme compression fiber to the centroid of 
the tension reinforcement)

The amount of composite action between the reinforcing steel and masonry is very
dependent on the workmanship during wall construction including the grout placement,
since the grout transfers the tension strength of the reinforcing steel into the wall. This
has been demonstrated in blast test programs on reinforced masonry walls, where walls
with careful inspection during construction demonstrated significantly greater blast
resistance than walls with no inspection (Oswald, et al 2006). Full composite action is
necessary for reinforced masonry to develop a ductile resisting moment based on the
dynamic tensile yield strength of reinforcement and the compression strength of the
masonry, as assumed for blast design.
All blast resistant reinforced masonry walls should be subject to inspection and material
testing during construction as required in Chapter 1 of TMS 402/ACI 530/ASCE 5 for
essential facilities (i.e. Level C Quality Assurance). This requirement helps ensure that
the reinforcing steel and surrounding grout will be constructed to act compositely with
the surrounding masonry before and after yielding of the steel and that there are no
voids in solid grouted walls that are intended to provide protection from fragments.
Procedures that inhibit full composite action include insufficient vibrating during
placement, improper reinforcing steel placement too near an edge of the grouted space,
mortar protrusion and droppings into the grouted space, and grout with insufficient
strength or plasticity. Additionally, both vertical and horizontal reinforcement should be
accurately positioned during wall construction and rigidly secured at intervals by wire
ties or spacing devices. The distance between reinforcement and the masonry unit
must not be less than -inch for fine grout or /-inch for course grout.
Ultimate Flexural Moment Capacity.
The ultimate dynamic moment capacity used to calculate the resistance of reinforced
masonry walls is shown in Equation 6-9. This equation assumes that reinforced
masonry will respond in essentially the same manner to blast loading as reinforced
concrete. The applicability of this assumption has been demonstrated in numerous
static tests and blast tests on well constructed reinforced masonry walls.
